White-browed scrubwrens (Sericornis frontalis) exhibit a life-history strategy broadly typical of small insectivorous passerines inhabiting temperate rainforests. The mass of a newly hatched chick is approximately 2.45 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.45 grams], placing the species within the expected range for acanthizid nestlings of its adult size. This initial mass is quite low relative to the ultimate body weights achieved by adults, a pattern common among altricial species that undergo a protracted period of rapid post-hatching growth supported by intensive biparental provisioning during the nestling phase.

Sexual dimorphism in body size becomes apparent as individuals approach adulthood, with the ultimate wet weight for females stabilizing at approximately 12.6 grams [Wwi = approximately 12.6 grams], while males attain a significantly larger adult mass of about 13.3 grams [Wwi = about 13.3 grams]. This modest degree of size dimorphism, with males being roughly five percent heavier than females, is thought to reflect sexual selection on male competitive ability during territory acquisition and mate defense. The magnitude of this difference is comparable to that reported for several other Sericornis species inhabiting similar mesic habitats. Body mass in adults shows relatively little seasonal fluctuation, although females may experience a measurable weight gain during egg formation, consistent with the energetic demands of producing a full clutch of eggs in this small-bodied passerine.

This relatively short nestling period reflects the species’ exposure to substantial nest predation risk, favoring rapid feather development and early departure from the nest. After fledging, the young remain dependent on parental care for an extended period. The reproductive biology of the White-browed scrubwren is characterized by a protracted breeding season and relatively modest annual output.
